utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we begin in the usual manner by taking the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Alex Demirdjian for the Prosecution, with Tom Hannis and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything that we need do in open session before we revert --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a small submission in relation to the motion upon which you partially ruled yesterday prior to the commencement of the testimony of this witness. Having been reminded of this motion, I reviewed it yesterday afternoon, and it is a motion that was filed on 8th of July seeking to amend our witness list in response to challenges to adjudicated fact. This motion was dealing with a number of witnesses, including witnesses from Kljuc, Teslic, Kotor Varos, et cetera, and I've noticed a typographical error. And considering that you may be ruling upon this motion shortly, I just wanted to bring this to your attention. At paragraphs 18 to 21, we deal with a witness from Teslic. And what we say in here is that he was already planned to be called by our motion of the 26th of May for adjudicated facts that were rejected by the 1st of April decision. However, what we requested in this motion is to expand his testimony as well. This was Witness ST-253 for Teslic. Requested to expand his testimony because the Zupljanin Defence were challenging Adjudicated Facts 1214, 1215, 1216, and 1218. And we said that this was an expansion upon the evidence that we sought to call which originally was in relation to Adjudicated Fact 560. And this is where the typographical error comes in. Adjudicated Fact 560 is in relation to the current witness, and there seems to have been an error in the motion at paragraph 21, so I will seek to make that correction right now. Instead of Adjudicated Fact 560, paragraph 21 of that motion should have Adjudicated Facts 500 to 503, as well as 504 to 505. You will find these in our original motion of the 26th of May in the annexes. In relation to Teslic, we had announced this witness, ST-253, for these two sets of adjudicated facts. I hope I haven't confused anybody with all these numbers, but these are the clarifications that I sought to make before we called the witness this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Demirdjian. The -- on the assumption that the -- what you have just explained clarifies everything, a close reading of the transcript should make it obvious as to what the correction should be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's correct. So we can call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And we are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we take the break and return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you again, sir. Now that we have settled on the mode in which you would give your testimony, there are a number of other preliminary questions which the Chamber would put to you before counsel for the Prosecution begins. The -- I assume that counsel for the Prosecution has a pseudonym sheet which I would invite the usher to pass to you, and if you're satisfied with the particulars on it, you would sign it and hand it back to her, please. So that is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1642, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And if we could go into private session, there are two questions that I have to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you -- well, we know from the earlier part of your examination that you have not testified previously before this Tribunal. And I would indicate to you, briefly, the procedure. That is, that the side calling - in this case, the Prosecution - would begin by asking you questions. And then the Defence would, for each of the accused, would have a right to question you, arising out of what you would have -- the answers you would have given in your questions to -- put to you by the Prosecution. And then the Prosecution would have a right to ask you questions arising out of their -- their questions. And when counsel are through, the Chamber -- or indeed at any earlier stage, the Chamber may have questions of you, and your -- that would then conclude your testimony. Ms. Pidwell, what I have before me, you have indicated four hours. Is that -- does that still hold?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And counsel for the Defence, what is your estimate of the length of time that your cross-examination would take?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we estimate that we need two sessions for this witness, maximum of three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... it is also our estimate, that we need two sessions to examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well the -- you would have heard what has -- what counsel has just -- the answers that counsel has just given in terms of the time that they expect to spend with you, so that gives you an idea as to how long you will be with us. But you needn't be alarmed that those would be continuous periods because A, for technical reasons having to do with the tapes by which the record is perpetuated and also to allow for the comfort of a witness, counsel, and everybody else, we do not sit for periods of longer than an hour and a half. And the -- and also, because the courtrooms have to be shared with other trials, we only sit for -- a morning session is either from 9.00 to 1.45; and if it's an afternoon session, it's from 2.15 to 7.00 in the evening. But as I said, that -- those sitting days are divided into session of no more than 90 minutes. You are beginning your testimony in the third and final session for today, so that we would be rising at -- for the day in an hour -- in -- in an hour and three minutes. And when we resume tomorrow afternoon, we are scheduled to begin in the afternoon at 2.15. So when your testimony -- when we adjourn today, your testimony will be continued at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. And with that, I would invite counsel for the Prosecution to begin.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, firstly I want to deal with your -- with history of your contact with the members of the Office of the Prosecution. Is it correct that the only time you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor was in Belgrade on the 25th of May this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And during the course of that interview, you had your lawyer present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: What was your lawyer's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jovo Dimitric.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And since your arrival in The Hague, have you been given the opportunity to read the transcript of that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And did you request any amendments or changes to be made to that transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. It was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going deal with the witness's background now, and I'd ask that we go into private session for that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was it your job to fill in this roster, or was it someone else's job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did that. It was my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And from these -- this duty roster, was it also part of your job description to compile reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, we made quarterly reports that were submitted to the Centre of Security Services, and I believe also the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: What were the nature of the quarterly reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they would give reports for the past three months for law enforcement, operative information collected, traffic accidents. But we had on our desk an instruction, how to make these reports. Sometimes they were written reports; sometimes they were statistical.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: How were these reports then transmitted to the CSB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe, at that time, by courier service. Part of the reports were sent by teletype, through the communications centre. And these are the two types of communication we had with the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Now, besides these rosters of duty that we've spoken about, what other records were required to be kept by -- by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many different records at the time. I wouldn't be able to remember them all, but we had that duty roster; then the record of people brought in, people detained; a record of fines collected; a record of crimes committed, including serious and less serious ones; record of misdemeanours with a breakdown into public order disturbances and traffic violations; and I think many other records.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And in the same way, were reports then compiled from these records for the CSB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You spoke about a record of people being brought in, people detained. What form did that take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were standardised forms in which you wrote in the information. You had just to write in the name and attach an Official Note, in case of a detention. All these standardised forms were filed in pursuant to the instruction, which said exactly how you fill in that form, what you write in each box. That's how we did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And in the case of someone being brought in, what information would you input into this form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If somebody was brought in, we had to indicate why, whether it was for the purposes of an interview, or at the request of a court or some other state authority. And therein lies the difference between "brought in" and "detained." People could be brought in with a warrant or without a warrant. A person can be brought in simply by exercising the authorisations that police officers have vested in them, without any warrant. Or they can be brought in on a warrant by the court or some other authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So if the person is brought in by a police officer without a warrant, this form is filled in. And then what are the standard procedures that then follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From those forms, the policemen on duty wrote a report addressed to the commander and the chief; and from that daily report, you can see all the work that was done by the police station for the past 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: In such a situation, who would make the decision to conduct an investigation or interview, rather, of the person who was brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Concerning people who were brought in without a warrant, just pursuant to basic police authority, the police officer who brought him in would fill in the form, or the officer on duty. If somebody was brought in on a court warrant, then the court would order specific policemen to bring in a -- the person to the court or some other agency. And once that is done, the police officer's job is -- is finished there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes. But on arrival at the police station, if someone's being detained without a warrant, who makes the decision to interview them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it depends. He was brought in -- that person was brought in perhaps for an interview by the Criminal Investigation Service, or maybe the chief wanted him, or one of the deputies. It's always written on paper why the person was brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did -- so did the chief actually conduct investigation -- interviews himself in some circumstances, or was that left to the Criminal Investigation Service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most often, interviews were conducted by the Criminal Investigation Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Where did those interviews take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All interviews with persons detained were conducted on the official premises of the -- of the agency that had the person brought in. If it was for the purposes of the Criminal Investigation Service, then in their offices. If the person was brought in for the requirements of the police, then in police stations. If the commander wanted that person to be brought in, then in his office.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And just to clarify, in your municipality, where were the offices of the Criminal Investigation Service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Upstairs. On the same floor as the office of the chief and the office of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So when you say "upstairs," you're meaning the SJB building itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: On that note, could you explain the various departments which made up the SJB in your municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the core service was the police; then there was a Criminal Investigation Service; traffic regulation; and the service for contacts with the citizenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Who did the heads of each of those services report to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the chief and to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: What were the requirements to report? Was it monthly or daily or ... are you able to provide us with any information on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the policemen on duty - and I'm talking about the times before the war - would report to the commander every morning. And after that report, he would submit also a written daily report that the chief would review. That was one way of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: How often was the head of the Criminal Investigation Service obliged to report to the chief or the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the morning briefing, these reports would be made to the chief over coffee.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm assuming from your answer you mean these are oral reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oral reports were made every morning; whereas written reports were submitted every three months. There were reports written for the requirements of the station and for the requirements of the centre, and also the republic level, Secretariat for Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could we go back into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Without naming these people, what was the responsibility of commanders in a substation to report to the overriding SJB under whose authority they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Substation police department were practically police stations in a micro area, and it was their duty to regularly, on a daily basis, report to the commander of the police station. It was their duty, too, to report on certain matters to the chief of the station. So they are police stations in a micro location.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You've said that there's an obligation to report, on a daily basis, to the commander but also, on certain matters, to the chief of the station. What are the certain matters that would require a commander of a substation to report to the chief, as opposed to the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the practice that information of interest acquired from operative work of interest for the work of the national or the state security would be conveyed by the commanders to the chief. At least that's how it was in my station.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: How would this be conveyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Person-to-person meetings, because they would usually meet every seven days. Or by using special telephone communications, secure telephones that operated from the station section to the police station, and police station to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can you please explain a little bit about how these special telephone communications worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Besides regular PTT lines, the public security station also had a special telephone. We used to call it the "specijal," the special, which was installed in the secretary's or the chief's office. And also in the substations; they would also have the same phones there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And what made this telephone line special?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A lot of information was protected at that time, which was of interest from the security point of view. So it was protected from being wire-tapped, because the phones could be tapped. And it was also used for urgent, quick information, if something needed to be reported quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And you said this -- this secure line was based in the office of the chief of the SJB. Do you know where, when he used it to call the CSB, where it was located in the CSB building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. But probably the CSB chief also had a special phone. Also probably the chief of the criminal investigation's police in Banja Luka did. These are special communications that existed in the organs of internal affairs at the time. As for who had them in Banja Luka, I don't know. I assume that if it was at some lower level, it would be in the office of the chief in the police station, and the chief of the centre too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you personally use this special line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember, but probably. I spoke from time to time with the chief of police in Banja Luka - not the chief of the centre, but the chief of the police - before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of something that was so urgent that it justified the use of this telephone, this special telephone, to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I noted already at the beginning about some information acquired throughout operations that was of interest for the work of the national security. Perhaps some urgent interventions. If something happened, if an employee was hurt while physical force or a rubber bat was used. So some events in the field of criminal work or traffic operations. Also some other confidential-type information too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So besides this special telephone line, what other means did you have to report to the CSB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, before we leave the special line, I would like to ask the witness how this special line was powered. Do you know? Did it run by the ordinary power system, or was it powered by a special generator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the telephones were connected through the PTT exchange, and some of the special lines -- actually, the special lines were protected in the PTT exchange. The president of the municipality, the president of the committee at that time, also had a special line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But my question was merely, What would happen if there was a power cut and no electricity available? Would the special line then still be operational?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a PTT connection. If we, in the police station, didn't have electricity, the phones would still be working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And would the PTT lines sometimes be broken off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I understand, we're still talking about the period before the war. So I don't recall any electricity cuts then. If there was, like, a regular power cut, we had a generator in the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sir, besides this -- this special telephone line, what other means did you have to report to the CSB in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could report through the communications system and through the PTT dispatch communications, as well as by the traditional messenger system, method.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When you say "the communications system," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant radio stations, fixed radio stations. And also via teleprinter. Some information that had to be protected would be sent through the teleprinter network, and they would be encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you say "the PTT dispatch communications," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that matter, there was a specific instruction, a document, about urgent, current, and periodical reporting, and I cannot remember right now what was implied by urgent, what was implied by current, and what by periodical type of reporting. But in any case, this instruction existed, and this flow of information was going from the police station, or the public security station, up to the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And just further to clarify, when you say that this flow of information is going up to the Security Services Centre by this PTT dispatch, is that a -- is that a telex, is that a dispatch, is it paper, is it -- can you please just clarify what that form of communication was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was written communication on paper. There would be a description of what was happening and then this would be typed into the teleprinter, if it was confidential information that the station was dispatching. And it was sent along the lines of operation. It would be sent to the police, the police section in Banja Luka, the criminal investigation police sector in Banja Luka, and then the relevant chiefs would communicate with each other, chief to chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Finally, you described the -- you used the phrase "a traditional messenger system." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By regular messenger post. There would be a courier with a brief-case going to Banja Luka monthly, bringing in the mail which would come from the republican SUP and also the mail that the centre was sending to us. And he would, in turn, also be delivering the mail that we were sending to the centre. This would be the messenger service.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was this service available on an urgent basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not always. It depends. If it was urgent, then it would be sent in the way I described. It would be done on the basis of the instructions. It would be done by dispatch, by special communication, the direct PTT line, and via personal contacts. If any of the superior officers would go to Banja Luka, to the centre, they would meet with their colleague over there. They would exchange information and agree on the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were you required to go to Banja Luka for face-to-face meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I would just go for the regular meetings of commanders and their deputies, not otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: How often would these regular meetings take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember. But it would be monthly, one meeting with commanders and deputies. The meetings were organised by the chief of the police department, when we're talking about the police. From time to time, these meetings were attended by the chief of the centre and by the police station chiefs. It all depended on the security assessment in the field at the time and the various actions that were ongoing, events.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was the chief of the SJB obliged to attend similar meetings at the CSB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were these separate from the meetings that you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police meetings would usually deal with the lines of operations, so I assume that the meetings would be held between chiefs, chiefs would go to see the chiefs of, let's say, the investigation -- Criminal Investigation Service and so on. And then you would also have meetings among the chiefs of stations and then the centres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we can go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I just want to ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I just want to ask you very briefly about the disciplinary measures that were available in your SJB. Perhaps we can take an example. If a police officer commits a crime during the course of his duty, could you explain the procedures that were required when that came to your attention.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, before the war, there were disciplinary commissions of the first degree at each public security station. And if what you referred to would happen, that authorised person would be suspended immediately, until the regular court proceedings were completed. The decision on the suspension would be made by the representative of the organ or, rather, the chief of the station. If a person was not satisfied with the first-instance commission decision, from what I can recall, there was a commission of the second-instance at -- at the station to which the person could appeal. And then that decision, which I think was signed by the chief of the centre, there was no longer any option for appeal other than bringing them before a regular court.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You spoke about the commission at the second-instance at the station. What did you mean by "the station"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at the station; but at the public -- at the security centre. So the first-instance one was at the SJB; and then the second-instance commission was at the CSB, from what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you talk about this commission, was it made up of several people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And who would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the idea was always for these people to be people of a -- with a university degree, with a high education, and that they be with a -- with a degree in law, actually. These were the criteria.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And would the chief of the SJB be part of this commission that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The chief of the SJB, as a representative of the station, would sign the final decision the commission made. If we were talking about suspension, if the employee was being suspended from the organ for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. I wonder if it's appropriate now to break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we've reached the point, Mr. Witness, when we would take the day's adjournment, as I indicated to you earlier. Having been sworn as a witness, you cannot now have any communication with counsel from either side. And in such communications, as in any conversations you have outside the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. So we will reconvene in this courtroom tomorrow afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 13th day of October, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
